title: High priest John kills his brother Jesus in the Temple; Bagoses defiles it
native: under 'another Artaxerxes' (Artaxerxes II); no year given
conversion: Josephus ties it to Artaxerxes II (404–358 BC), but the Elephantine papyri name Johanan as high priest and Bagohi as governor of Judah in 410–407 BC, so c. 410–400 BC.
note: Johanan (John) murdered his brother Jesus in the Temple; the Persian general Bagoses entered the sanctuary and laid a tax on every daily sacrifice for seven years.

title: Manasseh, brother of Jaddua, marries Sanballat's daughter
native: in the days of Darius III, before Alexander's invasion
conversion: Josephus places it just before Alexander's campaign (c. 335 BC); many scholars think he has displaced the Sanballat of Nehemiah's time (c. 430 BC).
note: The elders forced Manasseh to choose between his foreign wife Nikaso and the altar; he went over to his father-in-law Sanballat, who promised him a temple of his own.

title: Alexander the Great at Jerusalem bows before the high priest Jaddua
native: after the siege of Tyre and the taking of Gaza
conversion: Tyre fell in July/August 332 BC and Gaza about October; the visit would follow in late 332 BC. Many historians doubt the story.
note: Jaddua went out to Sapha (Mount Scopus) in his robes; Alexander bowed to the Name on his mitre, sacrificed in the Temple, was shown Daniel's prophecy of a Greek conqueror, and let the Jews keep their laws.

title: Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim built for Manasseh
native: Alexander 'permitted Sanballat ... to build' it during the siege of Tyre
conversion: Josephus dates it to 332 BC; Y. Magen's excavations on Gerizim place the first temple in the mid-5th century BC.
note: Sanballat built a temple like Jerusalem's on Gerizim and made Manasseh its high priest, the beginning of the separate Samaritan cult centre.

title: Ptolemy I takes Jerusalem on a Sabbath
native: 'he came into the city on a sabbath day, as if he would offer sacrifices'
conversion: No year given; dated 320 BC by most (Ptolemy's first seizure of Syria), others 312 or 302/301 BC. Day of the week known, date not.
note: Ptolemy son of Lagus entered on the Sabbath when the Jews would not fight, and carried many captives to Egypt; Josephus cites Agatharchides mocking the Jews for this.

title: Hezekiah the high priest goes to Egypt after the battle of Gaza
native: battle of Gaza 'in the eleventh year after the death of Alexander, and in the hundred and seventeenth olympiad'
conversion: Olympiad 117 = 312–309 BC; the battle of Gaza is securely 312 BC. Josephus is quoting Hecataeus of Abdera.
note: Hecataeus says Hezekiah, a Jewish chief priest about 66 years old, followed Ptolemy I to Egypt with many Jews; it shows the Jewish community in Egypt under the first Ptolemy.

title: Simon the Just becomes high priest
native: 'When Onias the high priest was dead, his son Simon became his successor. He was called Simon the Just'
conversion: Josephus makes him Simon I, son of Onias I (c. 300 BC); many scholars identify the Simon praised in Sirach 50 as Simon II (c. 200 BC).
note: Remembered for his piety and kindness to his people; the Mishnah names him one of the last of the Great Assembly.

title: Seventy-two elders translate the Law into Greek for Ptolemy II
native: under Ptolemy Philadelphus, Eleazar being high priest; finished 'in seventy-two days'
conversion: Ptolemy II reigned 283–246 BC; the translation of the Torah is usually dated c. 270–250 BC. Josephus follows the Letter of Aristeas.
note: At Demetrius of Phalerum's suggestion Ptolemy freed about 120,000 Jewish captives and asked Eleazar for six elders from each tribe, who translated the Law on the island of Pharos; this became the Septuagint.

title: Ptolemy III Euergetes sacrifices at the Jerusalem Temple
native: after he 'had gotten possession of all Syria by force'
conversion: After the Third Syrian War (246–241 BC); no year given.
note: Instead of thanking Egypt's gods, the king came to Jerusalem and offered many sacrifices according to Jewish law.

title: Joseph son of Tobias wins the tax farm of Syria and Judea
native: when Onias II refused tribute to 'Ptolemy Euergetes'; held it 22 years
conversion: Josephus names Euergetes (Ptolemy III, 246–222 BC), but his mention of Cleopatra suggests a later Ptolemy; c. 230 BC is a common estimate.
note: Joseph outbid the Syrian cities and collected the taxes for 22 years, making the Tobiad family the richest and most Hellenized house in Judea.

title: Antiochus III settles 2,000 Jewish families from Babylonia in Lydia and Phrygia
native: letter of Antiochus to Zeuxis, written when he 'was in the superior provinces'
conversion: Undated letter; usually set c. 210–205 BC during his eastern campaign.
note: The king moved loyal Jewish families from Mesopotamia to garrison rebellious Lydia and Phrygia, with land and ten years' tax relief; the start of the Jewish diaspora of Asia Minor.

title: Antiochus III takes Judea and issues a charter for the Temple
native: after Scopas was defeated at Panium
conversion: Battle of Panium 200 BC; the decree followed in 200–198 BC.
note: The Jews welcomed Antiochus; he granted Temple supplies, tax relief for the elders, priests and scribes, and forbade foreigners and unclean animals in the Temple.

title: Hyrcanus the Tobiad kills himself as Antiochus IV takes the throne
native: he ruled beyond Jordan seven years, all the time Seleucus reigned; died when Antiochus Epiphanes became king
conversion: Antiochus IV became king in 175 BC.
note: Hyrcanus built the fortified palace at Tyros (Iraq al-Amir, still standing) and killed himself fearing Antiochus.

title: Jason and Menelaus buy the high priesthood; gymnasium built in Jerusalem
native: 'upon the death of Onias ... they gave the high priesthood to Jesus his brother' (who called himself Jason)
conversion: Antiochus IV's accession, 175 BC (2 Maccabees 4).
note: Jason, then Menelaus, obtained the office from Antiochus; the Hellenizers built a gymnasium and hid their circumcision, the start of the crisis behind the Maccabean revolt.

title: Antiochus IV takes Jerusalem and plunders the Temple (143 SE)
native: 'in the hundred and forty-third year of the kingdom of the Seleucidae'
conversion: Seleucid year 143 = 169 BC (some 168 BC); on his return from Egypt.
note: Antiochus entered without a fight, killed many of the opposing party and carried off the Temple's golden altar, lampstand and table.

title: Mattathias kills the king's officer at Modein; revolt begins
native: no year in Josephus; follows the decrees of 145 SE
conversion: 1 Maccabees places it in 167/166 BC.
note: The priest Mattathias killed a Jew sacrificing on the pagan altar and the officer Apelles, overthrew the altar and called all who were zealous for the Law to follow him into the hills.

title: Antiochus IV desecrates the Temple (25 Kislev, 145 SE)
native: 'in the hundred forty and fifth year, on the twenty-fifth day of that month which is by us called Chasleu, and by the Macedonians Apelleus, in the hundred and fifty-third olympiad'
conversion: Seleucid year 145 on the spring (Babylonian/Jewish) era = 167/166 BC; Olympiad 153 = 168–165 BC; standard date December 167 BC. Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: The king built an idol altar on the altar of burnt offering, sacrificed swine, banned circumcision and the Sabbath, and martyred those who kept the Law. Josephus says this fulfilled Daniel's prophecy 'given four hundred and eight years before'.

title: Death of Mattathias; Judas Maccabeus takes command
native: 'when he had ruled one year'
conversion: One year after the revolt; 1 Macc 2:70 gives the 146th year = 166/165 BC.
note: Dying, Mattathias charged his sons to keep the Law and named Judas commander and Simon counsellor; he was buried at Modein.

title: Samaritans ask Antiochus IV to name the Gerizim temple for Zeus Hellenios
native: letter to Apollonius 'in the forty-sixth year, and the eighteenth day of the month Hecatombaeon'
conversion: Year 146 SE = 166 BC; Hecatombaeon is an Attic month (about July), so the day cannot be mapped securely to a lunar month; Julian date is the approximate start of that month.
note: To escape the persecution the Samaritans disowned kinship with the Jews and had their temple renamed for Jupiter (Zeus) Hellenios.

title: Death of Antiochus IV Epiphanes
native: 'This Antiochus died in the hundred forty and ninth year'
conversion: 149 SE = 164/163 BC; a Babylonian king list puts his death in late 164 BC.
note: After failing to rob a temple at Elymais he fell ill and died, confessing (Josephus says) that he suffered for sacrilege at Jerusalem; Lysias crowned the boy Antiochus V Eupator.

title: Judas Maccabeus rededicates the Temple: the Feast of Lights (Hanukkah)
native: 'dedicated anew, on the same day, the twenty-fifth of the month Apeliens, on the hundred and forty-eighth year, and on the hundred and fifty-fourth olympiad'
conversion: 148 SE (spring era) = 164 BC; Olympiad 154 = 164–161 BC; standard date December 164 BC. Josephus says the Temple lay desolate three years (1 Maccabees). Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: The lamps were lit on the new altar and an eight-day festival held; Josephus says the feast was called 'Lights' because liberty had shone on them unexpectedly. It is the earliest naming of Hanukkah as a feast of lights.

title: Antiochus V and Lysias besiege the Temple in a sabbatical year
native: 'in the hundred and fiftieth year of the dominion of the Seleucidae'; provisions failed 'because it was the seventh year'
conversion: 150 SE = 163/162 BC; the sabbatical year 164/163 BC lies behind the shortage. Peace was made in 162 BC.
note: Lysias besieged Mount Zion, but news of Philip's revolt made him grant peace; the king then broke his oath and pulled down the Temple walls. A key sabbatical-year anchor.

title: Menelaus executed at Beroea; Alcimus made high priest; Onias IV flees to Egypt
native: after the peace of 150 SE
note: Lysias had Menelaus killed as the cause of the troubles; Alcimus, not of the Oniad line, was made high priest, so Onias son of Onias III fled to Ptolemy VI.

title: Judas Maccabeus makes a treaty with Rome
native: after the death of Alcimus (as Josephus orders it)
conversion: The treaty (1 Macc 8) is dated 161 BC; Josephus wrongly makes Judas high priest after Alcimus.
note: Judas sent Eupolemus and Jason to the Senate, which declared the Jews friends and allies; the first Jewish–Roman treaty.

title: Judas defeats and kills Nicanor (Nicanor's Day, 13 Adar)
native: 'on the thirteenth day of that month which by the Jews is called Adar and by the Macedonians Dystrus'
conversion: Josephus gives no year; 1 Maccabees 7 places it in 151 SE = 161 BC (March). Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: Nicanor, who had threatened to burn the Temple, fell in battle with his 9,000 men; the Jews made the day an annual festival, the day before Purim.

title: Judas Maccabeus killed in battle at Elasa
native: no date in Josephus ('he had retained the high priesthood three years')
conversion: 1 Macc 9:3 gives the first month of 152 SE = spring 160 BC.
note: With only 800 men Judas fought Bacchides' army and fell; Jonathan and Simon buried him at Modein.

title: Onias IV builds a Jewish temple at Leontopolis in Egypt
native: petition to 'Ptolemy and Cleopatra' (Ptolemy VI Philometor)
conversion: Under Ptolemy VI (180–145 BC); usually c. 160–150 BC. Josephus says it stood 343 years (Jewish War 7.436), closed AD 73.
note: Onias cited Isaiah 19:19 ('an altar to the Lord in the midst of Egypt') and built a smaller copy of the Jerusalem Temple, served by priests until Vespasian closed it.

title: Jonathan puts on the high-priestly robe at Tabernacles
native: 'he put on the pontifical robe at the time of the feast of tabernacles, four years after the death of his brother Judas'; the 'hundred and sixtieth year'
conversion: 160 SE = 152 BC (1 Macc 10:21, seventh month); day taken as 15 Tishri, the first day of the feast. Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: Appointed by Alexander Balas, Jonathan became the first Hasmonean high priest, ending a vacancy Josephus elsewhere puts at seven years.

title: Jews and Samaritans argue before Ptolemy VI whose temple is lawful
native: before Ptolemy Philometor in Alexandria
conversion: Ptolemy VI reigned to 145 BC; c. 150 BC.
note: Each side staked its advocates' lives; the king ruled for Jerusalem and the Samaritan speakers Sabbeus and Theodosius were executed.

title: Josephus first names the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes
native: 'At this time there were three sects among the Jews'
conversion: Set in Jonathan's high priesthood (152–143 BC); c. 145 BC.
note: Josephus's earliest placement of the three schools, including the Essenes, who held that 'fate governs all things'; this is the period in which many date the Qumran community's origins.

title: Elephants turn on Ptolemy VIII's men; Alexandrian Jews keep a feast
native: 'when Ptolemy Physco ... exposed them naked and in bonds to his elephants'
conversion: Ptolemy VIII seized power on Philometor's death in 145 BC; the Jews of Alexandria kept the day as a festival (3 Maccabees tells a similar story under Ptolemy IV).
note: Onias and Dositheus had led Philometor's armies; when Physcon set drunken elephants on the Jews, the beasts trampled his friends, and the Jews kept the day as a feast of deliverance.

title: Trypho seizes and kills Jonathan
native: no year in Josephus
note: Trypho lured Jonathan into Ptolemais, held him for ransom, then killed him; Simon buried him at Modein and built the family monument of seven pyramids.

title: Simon frees Judea from Seleucid tribute: "first year of Simon"
native: 'after a hundred and seventy years of the kingdom of the Assyrians ... in their public records, they wrote, in the first year of Simon the benefactor and ethnarch'
conversion: 170 SE = 143/142 BC (1 Macc 13:41 'the yoke of the heathen was taken away').
note: The Jews began dating documents by Simon's years, the start of Hasmonean independence.

title: Simon takes the Acra and levels its hill
native: 'which cost them three whole years'
conversion: The citadel surrendered in 141 BC (1 Macc 13:51); Josephus adds that the hill was cut down over three years so the Temple stood highest.
note: The Seleucid garrison fortress that had dominated the Temple was demolished and its hill levelled.

title: Simon murdered by his son-in-law Ptolemy at a feast
native: no date in Josephus ('when he had been high priest eight years')
conversion: 1 Macc 16:14 gives the month Shebat of 177 SE = February 134 BC.
note: Ptolemy son of Abubus killed Simon and two of his sons at a banquet and held his wife; John Hyrcanus escaped and took power.

title: A sabbatical year halts Hyrcanus's siege of Dagon
native: 'that year on which the Jews used to rest came on; for the Jews observe this rest every seventh year'
conversion: First year of Hyrcanus, 135/134 BC; a key anchor for reconstructing sabbatical cycles (134/133 or 135/134 BC).
note: Hyrcanus lifted the siege for the sabbatical year; Ptolemy killed Hyrcanus's mother and brothers and fled.

title: John Hyrcanus opens David's tomb and takes 3,000 talents
native: at the end of Antiochus VII's siege
note: He used the silver to pay off Antiochus and was 'the first of the Jews' to hire foreign troops.

title: Antiochus VII besieges Jerusalem; truce for Tabernacles
native: 'in the fourth year of his reign, and the first year of the principality of Hyrcanus, in the hundred and sixty-second olympiad'; 'when the feast of tabernacles was at hand'
conversion: Antiochus VII's 4th year and Hyrcanus's 1st point to 134 BC; Olympiad 162 (132–129 BC) does not fit, an error in Josephus or his source. Day = 15 Tishri. Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: Hyrcanus asked a seven-day truce for the feast; Antiochus sent bulls with gilded horns for sacrifice, earning the name 'the Pious'. Rain fell 'at the setting of the Pleiades' to relieve the thirst of the besieged.

title: Antiochus VII's army halts two days at the Lycus for Hyrcanus's festival
native: Nicolaus: 'he staid there two days ... because it was such a festival ... whereon the law of the Jews did not allow them to travel' (Pentecost following a Sabbath)
conversion: Parthian campaign of 130 BC; the festival was Pentecost (early Sivan). Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: Josephus quotes Nicolaus of Damascus to show a Seleucid army respecting Jewish law.

title: Hyrcanus conquers Idumea and makes the Idumeans adopt Judaism
native: with the taking of Dora (Adora) and Marissa
conversion: c. 112–108 BC, alongside the Gerizim campaign.
note: The Idumeans could stay if they were circumcised and kept the Jewish law; Herod's family came from these converts.

title: John Hyrcanus destroys the Samaritan temple on Gerizim
native: 'which temple was now deserted two hundred years after it was built'
conversion: Traditionally dated 128 BC; Magen's excavations (coins) put the destruction at 112/111 BC, which is now standard.
note: Hyrcanus took Shechem and Gerizim and destroyed the temple that Alexander had allowed.

title: Hyrcanus breaks with the Pharisees and joins the Sadducees
native: late in his reign, after Eleazar's insult at a feast
conversion: No date; after his great victories, c. 110 BC.
note: Eleazar told him to give up the high priesthood because his mother had been a captive; Hyrcanus repealed Pharisaic ordinances, starting the long Pharisee–Hasmonean feud.

title: Hyrcanus's sons destroy Samaria; he hears a voice in the Temple
native: siege of one year; 'on the very same day on which his sons fought with Antiochus Cyzicenus'
note: While offering incense alone, Hyrcanus heard that his sons had just beaten Antiochus Cyzicenus, and it proved true; Samaria was razed.

title: Death of John Hyrcanus after 31 years
native: 'administered the government in the best manner for thirty-one years, and then died'
note: Josephus says God judged him worthy of three privileges: rule of the nation, the high priesthood and prophecy.

title: Aristobulus I becomes the first Hasmonean to wear a crown
native: 'first of all put a diadem on his head, four hundred eighty and one years and three months after the people had been delivered from the Babylonish slavery'
conversion: 104 BC by Hyrcanus's death; Josephus's 481 years would put the return in 585 BC, so the interval is unreliable.
note: He turned the high priesthood into a monarchy, imprisoned his mother and three brothers, and let her starve.

title: Judas the Essene's prophecy: Antigonus killed at Strato's Tower
native: during Aristobulus I's one-year reign, on 'the day' Judas had foretold
note: Judas, an Essene who 'never missed the truth in his predictions' and taught disciples in the Temple, foretold Antigonus's death at Strato's Tower; he was killed in a dark passage of that name in Jerusalem. Earliest named Essene in Josephus.

title: Aristobulus I dies; Ituraeans made to accept Judaism
native: 'when he had reigned one year'
note: He forced the Ituraeans of Galilee to be circumcised and died in remorse, vomiting blood.

title: Salome Alexandra frees Alexander Jannaeus and makes him king
native: after Aristobulus's death
note: Salome Alexandra, Aristobulus's widow, freed the brothers and made Jannaeus king and high priest (and, most think, married him).

title: Alexander Jannaeus takes and destroys Gaza
native: after a year's siege
conversion: c. 96 BC.
note: Treachery opened the city and Jannaeus's men sacked it.

title: Jannaeus pelted with citrons at Tabernacles; 6,000 killed
native: 'at the feast of tabernacles every one should have branches of the palm tree and citron tree'
conversion: No year; mid-reign, c. 94–90 BC. Month Tishri; day probably during the feast (15–21 Tishri). Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: As he stood at the altar the people threw their citrons and called him unfit to sacrifice as the son of a captive; he killed about 6,000 and built a wooden barrier round the altar.

title: Jannaeus crucifies 800 opponents in Jerusalem
native: after the war with Demetrius III Eucaerus
conversion: Demetrius's invasion is dated c. 88 BC; the crucifixions followed (88/87 BC).
note: Feasting with his concubines, Jannaeus had 800 Jews crucified and their families killed before them. The Qumran Nahum Pesher (4Q169) speaks of 'Demetrius king of Greece' and the 'Lion of Wrath' who 'hangs men alive', usually read as this event.

title: Death of Alexander Jannaeus at the siege of Ragaba
native: 'he died, after he had reigned twenty-seven years, and lived fifty years within one'
note: Dying, he told Alexandra to make peace with the Pharisees and give them power.

title: Hyrcanus II begins to reign
native: 'on the third year of the hundred and seventy-seventh olympiad, when Quintus Hortensius and Quintus Metellus, who was called Metellus of Crete, were consuls'
conversion: Hortensius and Metellus Creticus were consuls in 69 BC (Ol. 177.3 = 70/69 BC); this clashes with Alexandra's death in 67 BC, so Josephus may be dating Hyrcanus's high priesthood rather than his kingship.
note: Hyrcanus II held the kingdom only three months before his brother Aristobulus II took it.

title: Death of Queen Salome Alexandra after nine years
native: 'she died, when she had reigned nine years, and had in all lived seventy-three'
note: The Pharisees governed under her; her death left her sons Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II to fight for the throne.

title: Onias (Honi) the rain-maker stoned during the siege at Passover
native: 'As this happened at the time when the feast of unleavened bread was celebrated, which we call the passover'
conversion: Siege of Aristobulus II in the Temple by Hyrcanus II and Aretas III, spring 65 BC. Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: Asked to curse Aristobulus's party, Onias prayed that God would hear neither side and was stoned; the besiegers then cheated the priests of Passover sacrifices and a storm destroyed the crops.

title: Pompey hears Hyrcanus, Aristobulus and the people at Damascus
native: 'in the beginning of the spring' after his winter quarters
conversion: Spring 63 BC.
note: Three Jewish delegations came: the two brothers and the people, who asked to be rid of kings and governed by priests.

title: Pompey takes the Temple "on the day of the fast"
native: 'the city was taken on the third month, on the day of the fast, upon the hundred and seventy-ninth olympiad, when Caius Antonius and Marcus Tullius Cicero were consuls'
conversion: Consuls Antonius and Cicero = 63 BC (Ol. 179 = 64–61 BC). 'Third month' is the third month of the siege. Josephus's 'fast day' is taken as 10 Tishri (Day of Atonement); many scholars think it means a Sabbath (Dio says 'the day of Saturn'), putting it about June–July 63 BC. Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: Priests kept up the sacrifices while being cut down; about 12,000 Jews died. Pompey entered the Holy of Holies but touched nothing, and Judea became tributary to Rome.

title: Menahem the Essene greets the boy Herod as future king
native: when Herod 'was a child, and going to school'
conversion: Herod was born c. 73 BC; a schoolboy around 63–60 BC.
note: Menahem slapped the boy on the backside and told him he would be king and should love justice; when Herod later asked how long he would reign, Menahem said 'twenty or thirty years'.

title: Gabinius divides Judea among five councils
native: under Gabinius, proconsul of Syria
conversion: 57 BC.
note: After crushing Alexander son of Aristobulus he set up five synedria, ending Hasmonean monarchy; 'the people were glad to be freed from the rule of one man'.

title: Crassus plunders the Temple treasury
native: on his way to the Parthian war
conversion: 54 BC.
note: Crassus took the 2,000 talents Pompey had left and all the gold, about 8,000 talents, including a gold beam the priest Eleazar gave him on oath that he would take nothing else.

title: Consul Lentulus exempts Jewish Roman citizens of Asia from military service
native: 'This was done before the twelfth of the calends of October, when Lucius Lentulus and Caius Marcellus were consuls'
conversion: Consuls of 49 BC; a.d. XII Kal. Oct. = 19 September on the pre-Julian Roman calendar, which then ran some weeks ahead of the seasons, so the 'julian' value is the Roman civil date, not a true Julian date.
note: Lentulus released Jews with Roman citizenship from the levy 'on account of their religion', one of the decrees Josephus quotes to show Rome's protection of Jewish rights.

title: Julius Caesar confirms Hyrcanus II as ethnarch; Antipater a Roman citizen
native: decrees of Caesar after the Alexandrian war
conversion: 47 BC.
note: For their help in Egypt Caesar made Hyrcanus ethnarch, granted Antipater citizenship and freedom from tax, and let the walls of Jerusalem be rebuilt.

title: Caesar exempts the Jews from tribute in the sabbatical year
native: 'Caius Caesar, imperator the second time, hath ordained ... excepting the seventh, which they call the sabbatical year'
conversion: Caesar's 2nd imperatorial acclamation dates it to 47 BC (some put the decree in 44 BC).
note: Tribute was cut and remitted in sabbatical years, and Joppa restored to the Jews; evidence that the sabbatical year was observed.

title: Young Herod tried before the Sanhedrin for killing Hezekiah
native: Herod, governor of Galilee, 'but fifteen years of age' (probably 25)
note: Herod executed the bandit chief Hezekiah without trial; at the Sanhedrin only Sameas spoke out, warning that the man they acquitted would punish them all. Herod later killed the council except Sameas.

title: Antipater, Herod's father, poisoned by Malichus
native: after the death of Caesar, under Cassius
conversion: 43 BC.
note: Malichus had Hyrcanus's butler poison Antipater at a banquet; Herod had Malichus killed at Tyre.

title: The Roman Senate declares Herod king of Judea
native: 'having obtained it on the hundred and eighty-fourth olympiad, when Caius Domitius Calvinus was consul the second time, and Caius Asinius Pollio [the first time]'
conversion: Calvinus and Pollio were consuls in 40 BC (Ol. 184 = 44–41 BC; 184.4 = 41/40). Late 40 BC; a minority argue for 39 BC.
note: Antony and Octavian backed him; the Senate voted him king and he walked between the consuls to sacrifice on the Capitol.

title: Parthians install Antigonus as king; crowds gather for Pentecost
native: 'the enemy waited for the coming of the multitude out of the country to Pentecost, a feast of ours so called'
conversion: 40 BC. Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: The Parthians made Antigonus king; Phasael died, Hyrcanus's ears were cut off to bar him from the priesthood, and Herod fled to Masada and Petra.

title: Herod marries Mariamne, the Hasmonean princess
native: during the siege of Jerusalem, at Samaria
conversion: 37 BC (spring).
note: The marriage tied Herod to the royal house he was displacing.

title: Antony beheads Antigonus, the last Hasmonean king, at Antioch
native: Strabo: 'Antony ordered Antigonus the Jew to be brought to Antioch, and there to be beheaded'
conversion: 37 BC (late), or early 36 BC.
note: Josephus quotes Strabo that Antony was the first Roman to behead a king, to make the Jews accept Herod.

title: Herod appoints Ananel of Babylon high priest
native: first act after taking the kingdom
conversion: 37 BC.
note: Herod passed over the Hasmoneans and chose an obscure priest of the Babylonian diaspora, the first of many high priests appointed and removed by kings and Romans.

title: Herod and Sosius take Jerusalem "on the solemnity of the fast"
native: 'when Marcus Agrippa and Caninius Gallus were consuls of Rome on the hundred eighty and fifth olympiad, on the third month, on the solemnity of the fast ... on the same day ... after twenty-seven years' time'
conversion: Consuls Agrippa and Gallus = 37 BC (Ol. 185 = 40–37 BC), 27 years after Pompey. Josephus also says it was a sabbatical year (§475). Taken as 10 Tishri; some scholars prefer 36 BC (24 September 36 BC by the same method) or read 'fast' as a Sabbath in summer. Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: After a five-month siege the city fell and a massacre followed; Sosius dedicated a gold crown to God and took Antigonus to Antony. The end of Hasmonean rule.

title: Aristobulus III, the last Hasmonean high priest, drowned at Jericho
native: 'upon the approach of the feast of tabernacles ... When therefore the festival was over, and he was feasting at Jericho'
conversion: He was 17 and had served one year (35 BC). Month taken as Tishri, just after the feast. Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: The crowd's love for him at Tabernacles alarmed Herod, whose men held him under water in the palace pools 'in sport'.

title: Great earthquake in Judea in Herod's seventh year
native: 'in the seventh year of the reign of Herod ... there was an earthquake in Judea, such a one as had not happened at any other time'; Actium 'fell into the hundred eighty and seventh olympiad'
conversion: Spring 31 BC (Jewish War 1.370 'at the beginning of spring'), the year of Actium. The battle itself is already in the app.
note: About 10,000 people and many cattle died. Archaeologists (de Vaux) linked cracked cisterns and destruction at Khirbet Qumran to this quake.

title: Herod executes the aged Hyrcanus II
native: before Herod went to meet Octavian; Hyrcanus 'above fourscore years old'
conversion: 30 BC.
note: Accused of plotting with the Nabatean king Malchus, the last surviving Hasmonean ruler was put to death.

title: Octavian confirms Herod as king at Rhodes
native: after Actium
conversion: Spring 30 BC.
note: Herod laid aside his diadem and spoke frankly of his loyalty to Antony; Octavian restored it and later added Jericho, Gaza, Joppa and Strato's Tower.

title: Herod has Queen Mariamne executed
native: after his return from Octavian
conversion: 29 BC.
note: Falsely accused by Salome, Mariamne went to her death calmly; Herod, half-mad with grief, fell ill.

title: Herod institutes games for Augustus in Jerusalem
native: quinquennial games with theatre and amphitheatre
conversion: c. 28 BC.
note: Trophies in the theatre, thought to be images, caused outrage and a failed plot by ten citizens to kill Herod.

title: Herod refounds Samaria as Sebaste
native: named for Augustus (Sebastos)
conversion: 27 BC, the year Octavian took the name Augustus.
note: Settled with 6,000 colonists and given a temple to Augustus; Herod married Malthace and here later strangled two sons.

title: Famine in Herod's thirteenth year; Herod buys Egyptian grain
native: 'on this very year, which was the thirteenth year of the reign of Herod, very great calamities came upon the country'
conversion: 13th year from 37 BC = 25/24 BC.
note: Drought and plague; Herod melted his palace gold and silver to buy grain from Petronius, prefect of Egypt.

title: Herod makes Simon son of Boethus high priest and marries Mariamne II
native: to raise his bride's family
conversion: c. 23 BC.
note: The Boethus family, from Alexandria, held the office often afterwards and is linked by many to the Boethusians of rabbinic tradition.

title: Herod begins Caesarea Maritima at Strato's Tower
native: 'this city was thus finished in twelve years'
conversion: Begun c. 22 BC (dedicated 10/9 BC).
note: Herod built a harbour, Sebastos, larger than Piraeus, with a temple of Augustus and Rome.

title: Herod excuses the Essenes from the oath of loyalty
native: Herod 'had these Essens in such honor'; context of his 17th–18th year
conversion: c. 20 BC (Augustus's visit to Syria).
note: Herod demanded an oath of loyalty but excused Pollio, Sameas and the Essenes, whom Josephus likens to Pythagoreans, out of respect for Menahem.

title: Herod begins rebuilding the Temple in his 18th year
native: 'Herod, in the eighteenth year of his reign ... undertook a very great work, that is, to build of himself the temple of God'
conversion: 18th year from 37 BC = 20/19 BC; Jewish War 1.401 says the 15th year (23/22 BC).
note: He trained 1,000 priests as masons and enlarged the Temple Mount; work went on until AD 63/64 (John 2:20, 'forty and six years').

title: Herod's sanctuary finished; dedication falls on his accession day
native: 'the temple itself was built by the priests in a year and six months ... at the same time with this celebration ... fell also the day of the king's inauguration'
conversion: 18 months after 20/19 BC = c. 18 BC. The accession day is not given (from the capture of Jerusalem it may be 10 Tishri, but that is a guess).
note: Herod sacrificed 300 oxen; the porticoes took eight years. Josephus adds a tradition that rain fell only at night while the Temple was being built.

title: Marcus Agrippa sacrifices a hecatomb at the Jerusalem Temple
native: visit to Herod's kingdom
conversion: 15 BC.
note: Augustus's right-hand man feasted the people and sacrificed in the Temple; the next year he confirmed the rights of the Ionian Jews.

title: Caesarea dedicated in Herod's 28th year, Olympiad 192
native: 'The entire building being accomplished: in the tenth year, the solemnity of it fell into the twenty-eighth year of Herod's reign, and into the hundred and ninety-second olympiad'
conversion: Ol. 192 = 12–9 BC; 28th year = 10/9 BC.
note: Games for Augustus were held with gladiators and wild beasts, to recur every fifth year.

title: Herod robs David's tomb; two guards killed by a flame
native: after Hyrcanus had opened it before him
conversion: No date; c. 10 BC.
note: Herod took gold furniture by night; when his guards went deeper a flame burst out and killed two. In fear he built a white-marble monument at the entrance.

title: Herod's sons Alexander and Aristobulus strangled at Sebaste
native: after the trial at Berytus
conversion: 7 BC.
note: Mariamne's sons, condemned by a council under Saturninus, were strangled and buried at Alexandreion.

title: Over 6,000 Pharisees refuse the oath to Augustus and Herod
native: 'these very men did not swear, being above six thousand'
note: Pheroras's wife paid their fine; they foretold that Herod's line would lose the throne, and Herod killed several of them.

title: Joseph son of Ellemus serves as high priest for one day: "the fast"
native: 'there was another person made high priest for a single day, that very day which the Jews observed as a fast'
conversion: The fast is the Day of Atonement (10 Tishri) before Herod's death, most often taken as 5 BC; the eclipse that follows in the text is a separate night in spring. Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: Matthias the high priest became ritually unclean in a dream the night before, so his relative Joseph officiated that day only; the only such case Josephus records.

title: Death of Herod the Great at Jericho
native: 'he died, the fifth day after he had caused Antipater to be slain; having reigned, since he had procured Antigonus to be slain, thirty-four years; but since he had been declared king by the Romans, thirty-seven'
conversion: 37 years from 40 BC and 34 from 37 BC (inclusive) give 4 BC, between the eclipse and Passover (late March–early April). A minority argue for 1 BC.
note: After a terrible illness and the execution of Antipater, Herod died and was carried in state to the Herodium; his will divided the kingdom among three sons.

title: Judas son of Hezekiah, Simon and Athronges claim kingship
native: the disturbances after Herod's death
conversion: 4 BC.
note: Judas seized the arsenal at Sepphoris, Herod's slave Simon burned Jericho palace, and the shepherd Athronges wore a crown; 'Judea was full of robberies'.

title: Varus crucifies 2,000 rebels
native: 'the number of those that were crucified on this account were two thousand'
conversion: Summer/autumn 4 BC (the 'War of Varus').
note: The governor of Syria burned Sepphoris and Emmaus and crushed the revolt.

title: Augustus divides Herod's kingdom among Archelaus, Antipas and Philip
native: after hearing the delegations at Rome
conversion: 4 BC.
note: Archelaus became ethnarch of Judea, Samaria and Idumea; Antipas tetrarch of Galilee and Perea; Philip tetrarch of Batanea, Trachonitis and Auranitis.

title: Golden eagle torn down; Matthias burned alive the night of the eclipse
native: 'that very night there was an eclipse of the moon'
conversion: The eclipse is usually taken as 13 March 4 BC (already in the app), which fell at full moon in Adar (II) of that year. Alternatives: 9–10 January 1 BC or 15 September 5 BC.
note: Students of the teachers Judas and Matthias cut down Herod's golden eagle from the Temple gate; Herod had Matthias and others burned alive that night and deposed the high priest Matthias.

title: Archelaus's troops kill 3,000 at Passover
native: 'upon the approach of that feast of unleavened bread ... which feast is called the Passover'
conversion: Passover of 4 BC, just after Herod's death; day taken as 14 Nisan. Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: Mourners demanding punishment for Herod's executions filled the Temple; Archelaus's cavalry killed 3,000 and the feast was abandoned.

title: Pentecost revolt against Sabinus; Temple porticoes burned
native: 'on the approach of pentecost, which is a festival of ours, so called from the days of our forefathers, a great many ten thousands of men got together'
conversion: Pentecost 4 BC (early Sivan). Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: Pilgrims besieged the Roman procurator Sabinus; the Romans burned the porticoes and looted 400 talents from the Temple treasury.

title: Simon the Essene interprets Archelaus's dream; Archelaus banished
native: 'in the tenth year of Archelaus's government'; the summons came five days after the dream
conversion: 10th year from 4 BC = AD 6.
note: Archelaus dreamed of ten ears of corn eaten by oxen; Simon, 'of the sect of the Essens', said his ten-year rule was at an end. Five days later Augustus summoned him, and he was banished to Vienne.

title: Census of Quirinius; Judas the Galilean founds the "fourth philosophy"
native: 'the taxings ... which were made in the thirty-seventh year of Caesar's victory over Antony at Actium'
conversion: 37th year after Actium (Sept 31 BC) = AD 6/7. (Luke 2:2 is often reconciled with this census; the dating is debated.)
note: When Judea became a Roman province, Judas of Gamala and the Pharisee Saddok urged refusal of the tax as slavery, founding the movement Josephus blames for the war. Coponius was the first prefect.

title: Quirinius appoints Ananus (Annas) son of Seth high priest
native: after Joazar was deprived
conversion: AD 6; he held office until AD 15.
note: The Annas of the Gospels; five of his sons later held the office, which Josephus calls unique.

title: Josephus describes the Essenes (Antiquities 18)
native: in his account of the sects at the time of the census
conversion: Not an event; placed at AD 6 where Josephus's narrative introduces it. Written c. AD 93/94.
note: About 4,000 men who held property in common, did not marry or keep slaves, sent offerings to the Temple but sacrificed apart, and chose priests to prepare their food; he likens them to the Dacian Polistae.

title: Samaritans scatter human bones in the Temple at Passover
native: under Coponius, 'as the Jews were celebrating the feast of unleavened bread ... the priests ... open the temple-gates just after midnight'
conversion: Coponius governed AD 6–9; year uncertain (taken as AD 7). Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: Samaritans slipped in at night and defiled the porticoes, after which the Jews barred them.

title: Valerius Gratus appoints Joseph Caiaphas high priest
native: after Ishmael, Eleazar and Simon each held it about a year
conversion: Gratus governed AD 15–26; Caiaphas c. AD 18.
note: Caiaphas, son-in-law of Annas, held office about 18 years and presided at the trial of Jesus.

title: Tiberius expels the Jews from Rome; 4,000 sent to Sardinia
native: after the fraud on Fulvia
conversion: AD 19 (Tacitus, Annals 2.85).
note: Four Jewish swindlers took Fulvia's gifts for the Temple; Tiberius drafted 4,000 Jews for Sardinia.

title: Herod Antipas founds Tiberias
native: named for Tiberius
conversion: Coins date the founding to AD 19/20.
note: Built on a graveyard, so observant Jews thought it unclean; Antipas forced settlers to live there.

title: Pilate brings Caesar's images into Jerusalem
native: when he 'removed the army from Caesarea to Jerusalem, to take their winter quarters there'
conversion: Pilate came after Gratus's 11 years, AD 26; winter 26/27.
note: Crowds lay at Caesarea for five days and bared their necks to the swords; Pilate gave in and removed the standards.

title: Pilate builds an aqueduct with Temple money; protesters clubbed
native: 'Pilate undertook to bring a current of water to Jerusalem, and did it with the sacred money'
conversion: During AD 26–36; year unknown.
note: Disguised soldiers beat the protesting crowd with clubs, killing many.

title: Herod Antipas executes John the Baptist at Machaerus
native: no date; told as the cause of Antipas's defeat by Aretas (AD 36)
conversion: Josephus gives no year. The Gospels place it before the feeding of the 5,000 near Passover, about a year before the crucifixion: c. AD 31 on the app's AD 32 chronology (c. AD 28–29 on others).
note: Josephus says John was a good man who urged virtue and baptism, and that Antipas killed him fearing a rising; many Jews saw Antipas's defeat as God's punishment.

title: Josephus's passage about Jesus (the Testimonium Flavianum)
native: 'Now there was about this time Jesus, a wise man ... Pilate ... had condemned him to the cross'
conversion: Josephus dates it only 'about this time' under Pilate (AD 26–36). Placed at AD 32 to match the app's crucifixion (Ken Johnson); standard dates are AD 30 or 33. Most scholars think the passage is genuine at its core with Christian additions ('He was the Christ'); an Arabic version (Agapius) is more restrained.
note: Josephus calls Jesus a wise man and doer of wonderful works, condemned by Pilate at the urging of leading men, and says 'the tribe of Christians, so named from him, are not extinct at this day'.

title: Death of Philip the tetrarch in Tiberius's 20th year
native: 'in the twentieth year of the reign of Tiberius, after he had been tetrarch ... thirty-seven years'
conversion: Tiberius's 20th year = AD 33/34.
note: A just and quiet ruler, buried in the tomb he had built; his territory went to the province of Syria.

title: King Aretas IV defeats Herod Antipas
native: over Antipas's divorce of Aretas's daughter to marry Herodias
conversion: AD 36 (just before Tiberius's death).
note: Antipas's army was destroyed; Tiberius ordered Vitellius to make war on Aretas.

title: Pilate attacks the Samaritans gathered at Tirathaba
native: a man promised to show 'those sacred vessels which were laid under that place, because Moses put them there'
conversion: AD 36.
note: Pilate's cavalry killed many and executed the leaders; the Samaritans complained to Vitellius, which ended Pilate's career.

title: Pilate sent to Rome after ten years in Judea
native: 'Pilate, when he had tarried ten years in Judea, made haste to Rome ... but before he could get to Rome Tiberius was dead'
conversion: Late AD 36 / early 37; Tiberius died 16 March AD 37.
note: Vitellius sent Marcellus to take over and ordered Pilate to answer to the emperor.

title: Vitellius at Passover returns the high priest's robes and removes Caiaphas
native: 'it was at the time of that festival which is called the Passover'
conversion: Usually Passover AD 36 (some argue AD 37). Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: Vitellius gave the Jews custody of the vestments worn 'at the three yearly festivals, and on the fast day' and replaced Caiaphas with Jonathan son of Annas.

title: At a Jerusalem festival Vitellius learns of Tiberius's death
native: 'an ancient festival of the Jews being then just approaching ... on the fourth day letters came to him, which informed him of the death of Tiberius'
conversion: Spring AD 37, probably Passover (or Pentecost); Tiberius died 16 March AD 37 (already in the app).
note: Vitellius replaced Jonathan with his brother Theophilus, had the people swear allegiance to Gaius, and called off the war on Aretas.

title: Caligula frees Agrippa I and makes him king
native: after Tiberius 'held the government twenty-two years five months and three days'
conversion: AD 37.
note: Gaius gave Agrippa a gold chain as heavy as his iron one, Philip's tetrarchy and the title of king. An owl over him in prison had been read as a sign of rise, and of death when seen again.

title: Josephus born in Jerusalem
native: 'I was born to Matthias in the first year of the reign of Caius Caesar'
conversion: Gaius's first year ran from March AD 37 to March AD 38; he was 56 in Domitian's 13th year (AD 93/94), so AD 37/38.
note: Born to a priestly family of the first course with Hasmonean descent on his mother's side.

title: Herod Antipas and Herodias banished to Gaul
native: Gaius 'appointed Lyons, a city of Gaul, to be his place of habitation'
conversion: AD 39.
note: Accused by Agrippa of stockpiling arms, Antipas lost his tetrarchy; Herodias chose to share his exile.

title: Philo leads the Alexandrian Jewish embassy to Caligula
native: after the 'tumult ... at Alexandria'; Apion spoke for the Greeks
conversion: The riots were in AD 38; the embassy met Gaius in AD 39/40.
note: Gaius refused to hear Philo, who told his companions that the emperor had set God against himself.

title: Caligula orders his statue set up in the Temple; Jews refuse to sow
native: 'they continued firm ... and left off the tilling of their ground ... while the season of the year required them to sow it'
conversion: AD 40, autumn sowing season (some put the protest at Tiberias in AD 39/40).
note: Tens of thousands begged Petronius to kill them first; he risked death by delaying, Agrippa persuaded Gaius to withdraw the order, and Gaius's death in January 41 saved Petronius.

title: Some 50,000 Jews massacred at Seleucia
native: after the fall of Asineus and Anileus
conversion: c. AD 40 (the brothers' Nehardea state lasted about 15 years).
note: After the Jewish robber-princes Asineus and Anileus fell, Jews fled to Seleucia, where Greeks and Syrians killed more than 50,000.

title: Claudius gives Agrippa I Judea and Samaria
native: on Claudius's accession
conversion: AD 41 (Caligula's death is already in the app).
note: Agrippa, who had helped Claudius to the throne, now ruled the whole of Herod's kingdom; Claudius also issued an edict for the Alexandrian Jews.

title: Agrippa I begins the Third Wall of Jerusalem
native: Claudius, warned by Marsus, ordered it stopped
note: Built to enclose the new northern suburb (Bezetha); it would have made the city impregnable, Josephus says, had it been finished.

title: Young men of Dora set Caesar's statue in the synagogue
native: Petronius's edict quotes Claudius's recent decree
note: Agrippa protested and Petronius ordered the offenders arrested, upholding the Jews' right to their synagogue.

title: Agrippa I struck down at Caesarea during the games for Caesar
native: 'when Agrippa had reigned three years over all Judea'; 'on the second day of which shows he put on a garment made wholly of silver'; died after five days, 'in the fifty-fourth year of his age, and in the seventh year of his reign'
conversion: AD 44. The festival may be Caesarea's founding anniversary (5 March) or Claudius's birthday (1 August); no day can be fixed.
note: When flatterers hailed him as a god he did not rebuke them, saw the owl again, and died of pains in his belly; compare Acts 12:20–23.

title: Herod of Chalcis given power over the Temple and high priests
native: by Claudius after the vestments dispute
note: Herod king of Chalcis and his heirs could appoint high priests and manage the Temple treasury.

title: Theudas leads followers to the Jordan; beheaded by Fadus
native: 'while Fadus was procurator of Judea'
conversion: Fadus governed AD 44–46. Acts 5:36 sets a Theudas before Judas of the census, a known puzzle.
note: Claiming to be a prophet who would part the Jordan, he led a crowd with their goods; cavalry killed many, and his head was taken to Jerusalem.

title: Claudius lets the Jews keep the high priest's vestments
native: 'This letter is dated before the fourth of the calends of July, when Ruffis and Pompeius Sylvanus are consuls'
conversion: a.d. IV Kal. Iul. = 28 June; the suffect consuls Rufus and Pompeius Silvanus place it in AD 45. Roman calendar = Julian by then. Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: Fadus and Longinus had demanded the robes be kept in Antonia; the young Agrippa (II) won Claudius's consent that they stay with the Jews.

title: Great famine in Judea; Queen Helena of Adiabene brings food
native: 'Under these procurators [Fadus and Tiberius Alexander] that great famine happened in Judea, in which queen Helena bought corn in Egypt'
conversion: AD 44–48, usually AD 46–48 (perhaps worsened by the sabbatical year 47/48). Acts 11:28 places a famine under Claudius.
note: Helena, a convert to Judaism, bought grain in Alexandria and figs from Cyprus, and her son Izates sent money.

title: Tiberius Alexander crucifies James and Simon, sons of Judas the Galilean
native: 'the sons of Judas of Galilee were now slain'
conversion: Tiberius Julius Alexander governed AD 46–48.
note: The founder's sons kept his movement alive; Tiberius Alexander, an apostate nephew of Philo, had them crucified.

title: A Roman soldier's insult at Passover ends in a deadly crush
native: 'on the fourth day of the feast, a certain soldier let down his breeches, and exposed his privy members to the multitude'
conversion: Cumanus governed AD 48–52; usually dated AD 49 (year not given). 4th day of Unleavened Bread = 18 Nisan. Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: Stones were thrown, Cumanus brought in troops, and in the panic in the narrow passages about 20,000 died (Jewish War says 30,000).

title: A soldier tears up a Torah scroll; Cumanus beheads him
native: after the robbery of Caesar's slave Stephanus
note: To calm the outcry Cumanus had the soldier executed.

title: Galilean pilgrim killed at Ginae; Cumanus deposed by Claudius
native: a Galilean going up 'to the festival' was killed
note: Jewish reprisals, Cumanus's bribery and Quadratus's inquiry led Claudius, persuaded by young Agrippa, to execute Samaritan leaders and banish Cumanus.

title: Felix, brother of Pallas, made procurator of Judea
native: after Cumanus
conversion: AD 52.
note: Felix later married Drusilla, Agrippa II's sister, and heard Paul (Acts 24).

title: Claudius gives Agrippa II the tetrarchy of Philip in his twelfth year
native: 'when he had already completed the twelfth year of his reign, he bestowed upon Agrippa the tetrarchy of Philip and Batanea'
conversion: Claudius's 12th year ended January AD 53.
note: Agrippa II lost Chalcis but gained a larger kingdom; he ruled until the end of the century.

title: Josephus tries the three sects and lives three years with Banus
native: 'when I was about sixteen years old ... Banus ... lived in the desert'; returned 'in the nineteenth year of my age' and followed the Pharisees
conversion: Age 16 from AD 37/38 = AD 53/54; with Banus until about AD 56/57.
note: Josephus says he went through the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes, then lived with the ascetic Banus in the desert, wearing what grew on trees and bathing often in cold water.

title: Helena and Izates buried in pyramids near Jerusalem
native: Izates 'died ... when he had reigned twenty-four years'; Helena soon after
conversion: c. AD 55–58 (Izates acceded c. AD 36).
note: Their bones were laid in three pyramids three furlongs from the city, usually identified with the 'Tomb of the Kings'.

title: The sicarii murder the former high priest Jonathan
native: on Felix's prompting
conversion: During Felix's term (AD 52–59/60); c. AD 56.
note: Jonathan son of Annas criticised Felix, who had the sicarii stab him; their daggers in festival crowds began a run of killings.

title: The "Egyptian" prophet leads a crowd to the Mount of Olives
native: promised the walls of Jerusalem would fall at his command
conversion: Under Felix, c. AD 56; Acts 21:38 mentions him.
note: Felix killed 400 and took 200 prisoners; the Egyptian escaped and was never seen again.

title: Porcius Festus succeeds Felix
native: 'Upon Festus's coming into Judea'
conversion: AD 59 or 60.
note: Festus fought the sicarii and an impostor in the wilderness; he heard Paul's appeal to Caesar (Acts 25).

title: Nero rules for Caesarea's Greeks against its Jews
native: Burrhus was bribed to obtain the letter
note: The decision on citizenship rights at Caesarea, Josephus says, 'afforded the grounds of the miseries that followed' and led to war.

title: Priests wall off Agrippa II's view; Poppaea wins Nero's consent
native: 'This was granted them in order to gratify Poppea, Nero's wife, who was a religious woman'
note: The priests built a wall to block the king's dining room from seeing into the Temple; Nero let it stand, keeping the high priest Ishmael as hostage.

title: James, "the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ", stoned
native: 'Festus was now dead, and Albinus was but upon the road; so he assembled the sanhedrim of judges, and brought before them the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James'
conversion: Between the death of Festus and the arrival of Albinus: AD 62. Hegesippus (Eusebius) places it just before Vespasian's siege; Josephus is earlier.
note: The new high priest Ananus son of Annas, a Sadducee, had James and others stoned; protesting citizens had Agrippa II depose him after three months. The passage is widely accepted as genuine.

title: Josephus sails to Rome at 26; shipwreck and Poppaea
native: 'when I was in the twenty-sixth year of my age, it happened that I took a voyage to Rome'
conversion: 26th year of age from AD 37/38 = AD 63/64.
note: Going to free priests Felix had sent to Rome, he survived a shipwreck with about 80 of 600 aboard; through the actor Aliturus he met Poppaea, who freed them.

title: Agrippa II lets the Levite singers wear linen like the priests
native: 'that he might have a memorial of such a novelty'
note: Josephus sees this breach of ancestral law as one cause of the coming disaster.

title: Herod's Temple finally completed; 18,000 workmen idle
native: 'And now it was that the temple was finished'
conversion: Under Albinus (AD 62–64), c. AD 63/64, about 83 years after it was begun and six years before it was burned.
note: To give work to more than 18,000 men, Agrippa had the city paved with white stone.

title: Gessius Florus made procurator through Poppaea
native: 'sent as successor to Albinus by Nero'
conversion: AD 64.
note: His wife Cleopatra was a friend of Poppaea; Josephus says Florus's greed drove the Jews to war.

title: The Jewish war with Rome begins
native: 'this war began in the second year of the government of Florus, and the twelfth year of the reign of Nero' (the month Artemisius is given in Jewish War 2.284)
conversion: Nero's 12th year (Oct 65–Oct 66) and Florus's 2nd = AD 66; Artemisius = Iyar (Jewish War 2.284 adds 'the seventeenth year of Agrippa'). Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.
note: Riots at the Caesarea synagogue and Florus's seizure of Temple money set off the revolt that ended with the Temple's destruction in AD 70.

title: Vespasian gives Josephus his house, citizenship and a pension
native: 'when we were come to Rome ... he gave me an apartment in his own house ... honored me with the privilege of a Roman citizen'
conversion: On arrival with Titus, AD 71.
note: Josephus lived in Vespasian's old house and received lands in Judea; he wrote his histories there.

title: Josephus presents the Jewish War to Vespasian and Titus
native: 'Titus was so desirous that the knowledge of these affairs should be taken from these books alone, that he subscribed his own hand to them'
conversion: Before Vespasian's death (June AD 79); usually AD 75–79.
note: Agrippa II wrote 62 letters vouching for it; Titus ordered it published.

title: Josephus completes the Antiquities in Domitian's 13th year
native: 'which is the thirteenth year of the reign of Caesar Domitian, and the fifty-sixth year of my own life'
conversion: Domitian's 13th year = Sept AD 93–Sept 94.
note: Twenty books of Jewish history from Creation to the eve of the war; the Life was added as an appendix.

title: Against Apion names 22 sacred books, prophecy ending with Artaxerxes
native: 'only twenty-two books, which contain the records of all the past times'
conversion: Written after the Antiquities, c. AD 94–100.
note: Five books of Moses, thirteen of the prophets and four of hymns and precepts; books after Artaxerxes were not trusted equally because 'there hath not been an exact succession of prophets'. The earliest Jewish list of the canon.
